MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
The route is the part with real constraints, so I'll start there. **There's only one order that works, B → A → C, and it gets the van back at exactly 12:00, with no slack.**

## Route and timeline

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B. Done 25 min before the shop opens at 09:30 |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A, inside the 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-min break**, parked near C |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C, as soon as the office accepts deliveries |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | Back at depot |

**Why no other order works:**
- **A first:** finishing at A at 09:15 and driving 25 minutes gets the van to B at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- **C before A:** C can't take delivery until 11:00, and A's window closes at 10:00.
- **B first** is therefore forced, and A has to come before C.

**The risk: zero buffer on the return.** Because C can't start before 11:00, the earliest the van can get back is 11:00 + 15 + 45 = 12:00, whatever time it leaves. Any delay at C, such as a slow handover, the office not ready, or traffic, makes it late. Three ways to protect it:
- Call office C the day before to make sure someone will be there at 11:00 sharp.
- Ask whether the 12:00 return can slip if needed.
- Move C to another day if the deadline is fixed.

There is slack elsewhere. The break fits in the wait before C, and B has 25 minutes of margin.

## Van name (staff vote)

- **Dovetail**
- **Sandy**
- **French Polish**
- **The Chesterfield**
- **Patina**

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Business]. I'm about [15] minutes away with your furniture. See you soon!

## Three checks before handover

1. **Condition:** no new marks, chips or scratches from transit. Compare against the photos taken before loading.
2. **Function:** drawers and doors open smoothly, hardware is tight, and the piece sits level and stable.
3. **Completeness:** it's the right item, with every part included: shelves, keys, feet, glass, cushions.

## Paper or emailed delivery note

**Emailed by default.** It's harder to lose, can include the condition photos, and gives you a searchable record. Keep paper available for customers who ask for it or don't have email.

## Proof of delivery (for the part-timer)

> Proof of delivery is our record that the item was handed over in good condition: the customer's signature or name, the date and time, and photos of the piece on arrival.

## Evening-before text

> Hi Sam, your furniture from Hale Restoration arrives tomorrow 9:00-10:00. We'll text when the driver sets off. Any problems, call 01234 567890. Thanks!

With those sample details it's **151 characters**. Longer names or business names will push it up, so trim "Thanks!" or "Any problems," if you need space.

Use a plain apostrophe (') and no emojis. Curly quotes or emojis can switch the message to a format where the single-message limit drops to 70 characters, so it would be sent as several texts.
